name: Dry cooler

sources.title: TechTarget on Schneider Electric 32 C vs 45 C TCS modeling in Dallas and Paris

summary: Fans blow outdoor air over a finned coil; the water can only get to a few kelvin above the outdoor dry-bulb temperature. Uses no water and little power, so it pairs with warm-water liquid cooling. On hot hours it needs a trim chiller.

approachK.note: Schneider's 100 MW model (Dallas, Paris) starts chiller assist at ~25 °C outdoor for a 32 °C supply and ~35 °C for 45 °C supply: approach of 7 to 10 K. Larger coils reach 5 K at higher capex.

copRef.note: No compressor; trim cooling uses the chiller entry's curve.

fanPowerFraction.note: EC-fan V-coil dry coolers at design duty draw roughly 15 to 30 kW of fan power per MW rejected; less at part load.

waterLPerKwh.note: Sealed closed loop, sensible heat only.

unitCapacityW.note: Data-center V-coil dry coolers are sold from 150 kW to 1.8 MW (LU-VE) and up to 2.5 MW (ENEX); 1 MW is a typical unit at warm-water conditions.

capexUsdPerKw.note: Coil-and-fan equipment without compressors; cheaper per unit than a chiller but large coil area for small approach. No primary cost source found.

leadTimeWeeks.note: Shorter than chillers (no compressors) but caught in the same 2025-26 cooling backlog that Linesight flagged.

installWeeks.note: Roof or yard set, piping and controls.

footprintM2PerMw.note: A 1 MW V-coil unit is roughly 12 x 2.3 m; 7 K approach needs more coil per MW than a chiller condenser, plus spacing to avoid hot-air recirculation.
